lesson.title: Reading the Entropy of a Substance Off a Table
lesson.summary: Unlike enthalpy, entropy has a true absolute zero point, so every substance has a standard molar entropy, S degree, that can be looked up directly and combined for reactants and products to get delta S of reaction without needing any intermediate equations.
lesson.body:
Enthalpy has no natural zero: tables report enthalpies of formation relative to elements in their standard states, an arbitrary but useful reference point. Entropy is different, because of the third law of thermodynamics, which states that a perfect crystal at a temperature of absolute zero has an entropy of exactly zero, since at 0 K, with no thermal motion at all, there is only one way to arrange a perfectly ordered crystal. That gives entropy an actual absolute reference point, which means chemists can tabulate the true, absolute molar entropy of any substance at any temperature, most commonly at 298 K and standard pressure, written S degree, in units of J/(mol K). This is a meaningfully different situation from enthalpy of reaction, where you generally had to combine multiple thermochemical equations through Hess's law to get anywhere. For entropy, you can often just look up a single number per substance and combine those numbers directly.

The formula follows the same products-minus-reactants pattern used throughout thermochemistry: delta S degree (reaction) = the sum of moles times S degree for every product, minus the sum of moles times S degree for every reactant. Because these are absolute values rather than reaction-specific measurements, there is no need to reverse or scale separate equations the way Hess's law calculations required; you simply plug tabulated values for each species, weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient, straight into the formula.

As a worked example, consider the Haber synthesis of ammonia, N2(g) + 3 H2(g) -> 2 NH3(g). Using commonly tabulated standard molar entropy values, which vary slightly between reference sources but are broadly consistent, S degree(N2) is about 191.6 J/(mol K), S degree(H2) is about 130.7 J/(mol K), and S degree(NH3) is about 192.8 J/(mol K). Products: 2 mol NH3 x 192.8 J/(mol K) = 385.6 J/K. Reactants: (1 mol N2 x 191.6 J/(mol K)) + (3 mol H2 x 130.7 J/(mol K)) = 191.6 + 392.1 = 583.7 J/K. Subtracting: delta S degree = 385.6 - 583.7 = about -198.1 J/(mol K).

The negative sign is worth pausing on rather than just accepting. The reaction converts 4 total moles of gas (1 mole of N2 plus 3 moles of H2) into 2 total moles of gas (NH3). Fewer, more constrained gas particles on the product side means fewer ways to distribute their positions and momenta, so the system's entropy decreases even though the reaction is exothermic. This is a good preview of the reasoning developed further in the entropy and disorder chapter: entropy tracks with the number of gas molecules and the freedom they have, not with whether a reaction gives off heat. It is also a good example of why chemists need both delta H and delta S, and eventually delta G, to fully predict whether and under what conditions a reaction will proceed, since a reaction can be enthalpically favorable while being entropically unfavorable at the same time, exactly as ammonia synthesis is.
